JSON: Name: mdm_wdm_photonic_processor Title: Hybrid mode-division and wavelength-division photonic processor for low-latency optical MIMO signal unscrambling and RF unjamming Short Hypothesis: A monolithically integrated photonic processor that combines mode-division multiplexing (MDM) with wavelength-selective microring resonator (MRR) weight banks and balanced multimode photodetectors reduces end-to-end optical processing latency to below 50 ps and increases operations-per-second per mm2 by at least 3x relative to an equivalent WDM-only MRR processor while recovering scrambled 5 Gb/s NRZ channels with bit-error-rate below 1e-4. Related Work: Existing photonic matrix-vector multiply and MIMO processors primarily follow three approaches: wavelength-division-multiplexing (WDM) with microring weight banks, spatial/MZI interferometer meshes (coherent SDM), and time-division schemes. WDM+MRR systems offer compact, phase-insensitive weighting but are limited by microring free-spectral-range (FSR) which constrains usable wavelength channels and hence scalability; they also require a large number of rings for high-dimensional problems and suffer increased optical loss and tuning overhead as scale grows. MZI mesh / coherent SDM implementations provide programmable unitary transforms but are phase-sensitive, require complex phase control, are bulky, and are sensitive to thermal and fabrication variability. TDM approaches shift complexity to ultrafast modulators and electronics, increasing synchronization and power demands. Prior MDM demonstrations have used off-chip components or required demultiplexing and per-channel detection before electronic summation, preventing direct multimode optical addition and increasing footprint and latency. Across these approaches unresolved issues include limited on-chip multiplexing capacity, scalability tradeoffs between optical/electrical capacitance and throughput, lack of integrated balanced multimode detection for direct optical summation, and FSR- or phase-limited channel reuse. Abstract: We target scalable, low-latency analog photonic processing for high-throughput MIMO and RF interference mitigation by integrating spatial and spectral multiplexing on a single chip. We propose and implement a hybrid architecture that combines adiabatic mode multiplexers, mode-selective microring resonator weight banks, and balanced multimode photodetectors to perform wavelength- and mode-resolved weighting and direct optical summation without per-channel electronic demultiplexing. The primary contribution is a monolithic MDM–WDM photonic processor architecture that reuses N wavelengths across M orthogonal spatial modes to scale weight capacity by M while preserving incoherent, phase-insensitive operation and enabling negative weights and direct multimode addition. Expected outcomes are sub-50 ps optical processing latency, substantially higher operations-per-second per unit area than WDM-only processors, and demonstration of real-time optical MIMO unscrambling and RF unjamming at multi-gigabit rates within an analog optical domain. Experiments: Datasets: 1) Optical data streams: PRBS length 2^13-1 NRZ at 5 Gb/s for two spatial modes (TE0, TE1) and for scaling tests up to 4 modes; 2) RF data streams: BPSK and QPSK modulated carriers (carrier 2.565 GHz) with broadband jammer samples drawn from uniform distribution spanning 2.5 GHz; 3) Simulated channel ensembles: randomized unitary and non-unitary mixing matrices with controlled mode-dependent loss and modal crosstalk levels (0–20 dB) for Monte Carlo evaluation. Baselines: A) WDM-only microring weight bank processor with equivalent number of wavelength channels; B) coherent MZI mesh implementation sized for equivalent MVM dimensions; C) electronic DSP BSS implemented on FPGA (reference optimized implementation); D) WDM with spatial-multiplexed electrical summation (WDM-SMS). Metrics: BER, Q-factor, optical processing latency (ps), ops/sec/mm^2 (OPS/mm^2), energy per MAC (pJ/MAC), insertion loss (dB), intermodal crosstalk (dB), photodetector responsivity (A/W), detector 3-dB bandwidth (GHz), MRR extinction ratio, MRR tuning power (mW), reconfiguration time (Hz). Experimental setup: tunable narrow-linewidth laser(s) for each wavelength; Mach-Zehnder modulators driven by AWG for data and pilot insertion; polarization controllers and mode launch optics to excite TE0–TE3; on-chip adiabatic mode multiplexer and mode-selective MRR weight bank with thermal heater drivers instrumented for power measurement; balanced multimode germanium-on-silicon PIN photodetectors reverse biased at 3 V; high-speed oscilloscope (≥50 GSa/s) and real-time scope for BER/Q and eye diagrams; optical spectrum analyzer (0.01 nm resolution) for MRR spectra; temperature-controlled stage. Primary experiments: 1) Reproduce on-chip optical unscrambling: program thermal MRRs using pilot-based unmixing to implement A^-1 for two-mode, two-wavelength configuration; measure BER vs input optical power (-10 to 0 dBm), Q-factor, eye diagrams, and optical processing latency (impulse response method). 2) RF unjamming: impose broadband jammer on PSK/QPSK target, perform blind source separation (FastICA and pilot methods) to estimate mixing and program MRRs; measure constellation improvement and Q-factor pre/post unjamming, bandwidth throughput (GHz), and latency. 3) Scaling study: vary M from 1 to 4 (and simulate to 8–10) modes while holding wavelength count fixed; measure OPS/mm^2, BER, insertion loss, and detector loading. 4) Ablation studies: A) replace balanced multimode PD with demultiplex+single-mode PDs summed electrically (evaluate BER, latency, OPS/mm^2); B) disable MDM (WDM-only) and compare scaling of OPS and BER; C) vary modal crosstalk in simulated ensembles to quantify BER sensitivity. 5) Compare against baselines A–D on identical test signals and identical input power ranges. Data analysis: report mean and 95% confidence intervals across ≥100 randomized channel instances; compute ops/sec/mm^2 from measured photonic MAC throughput and die area; energy-per-MAC including static MRR heater power and detector drive where appropriate. Risk Factors and Limitations: Fabrication variability: deviations in waveguide dimensions and ring coupling coefficients can degrade mode selectivity and MRR extinction, increasing crosstalk and insertion loss. Modal crosstalk and non-ideal orthogonality: mode-dependent loss and imperfect mode conversion reduce recovery fidelity and may violate BSS independence assumptions, degrading separation performance. MRR FSR and thermal tuning limits: finite FSR constrains usable wavelength grid and thermal tuning consumes static power and has limited speed and precision; tuning resolution limits achievable weight precision. Photodetector bandwidth and capacitance: multimode detector geometry required to support many modes increases junction capacitance and can reduce electrical bandwidth, affecting achievable OPS and requiring tradeoffs between responsivity and speed. Scaling trade-offs: supporting larger numbers of spatial modes requires wider waveguides and larger detectors, increasing chip area and potentially raising optical loss and electrical parasitics that diminish throughput gains. Pilot overhead and BSS assumptions: pilot insertion reduces net payload throughput; statistical BSS methods assume source independence and non-Gaussianity which may not hold for all real-world signals, limiting generalization. Thermal crosstalk and packaging: heater-induced thermal crosstalk and packaging constraints may limit dense integration and reconfiguration fidelity. Noise floor and dynamic range: low optical input power or elevated detector noise may push signals to noise floor, limiting BER performance. Integration complexity: combining high-density MRR arrays with driver electronics and heat management on-chip increases system complexity and may complicate manufacturability and yield.
